blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The Mesolithic Age serves as a transitional phase between the Paleolithic and Neolithic periods.
The era is characterized by the production of microliths—small, refined stone tools attached to bone or wooden handles.
Earliest evidence of animal domestication in India emerges during this period, notably at Bagor and Adamgarh.
Human lifestyle shifted from pure hunting-gathering to semi-sedentary living with fishing and herding.
Prehistoric cave rock art flourished, vividly depicting hunting scenes, dancing, and social life.

blocks.content: The Mesolithic Age lasted roughly from 10,000 BC to 6,000 BC.
The Mesolithic Age represents a critical transition in human history from hunting and gathering toward animal domestication and settled life.
The Mesolithic Age represents a transitional phase between the Paleolithic and Neolithic ages. - Humans still hunted animals
but began to adopt more efficient techniques. - This period shows early signs of settlement near water sources.

rows: Crude, unpolished large stone tools (hand axes, cleavers)
Hunting, gathering, fishing, and early animal domestication

items: The most important tools were microliths, which were very small and finely made stone tools.
These tools were often used as arrowheads, spear points, and sickles. One-liner for : Microliths belong to the Mesolithic Age.
People hunted animals and also started fishing.
Temporary settlements developed near rivers and lakes.
Microliths (1 cm to 8 cm stone tools, often geometric) are uniquely associated with the Mesolithic Age.
Bagor in Rajasthan and Adamgarh in Madhya Pradesh provide the earliest evidence of animal domestication in India.
Bhimbetka rock shelters in Madhya Pradesh contain extensive Mesolithic paintings depicting hunting and social activities.
Cave paintings continued but became more detailed.

blocks.content: Important Mesolithic sites: - Bhimbetka (Madhya Pradesh) - Bagor (Rajasthan)
